title: Count set bits
instructorPromptText: Write a C function `int count_set_bits(unsigned int n)` that counts and returns the number of set bits (1s) in its binary representation using bitwise operators (`&`, `>>`).

specGateDimensions.description: Does the function strictly use bitwise operators (like `& 1` and `>>= 1`) instead of arithmetic operations (like `% 2` and `/ 2`)?
specGateDimensions.rationale: Forces direct bit-level manipulation, reinforcing low-level processor execution models.

specGateDimensions.description: Does the function signature match `unsigned int` to ensure shift operations behave as logical shifts rather than arithmetic shifts?
specGateDimensions.rationale: Signed integer shifts carry sign bit extensions, which can cause infinite loops or incorrect bit counts for negative values.

specGateDimensions.description: Does the counting loop terminate correctly when the value reaches zero?
specGateDimensions.rationale: Terminating early when no more bits are set is more efficient than always iterating 32 times, though both are technically correct.

expectedDivergences.pattern: Student uses arithmetic modulo `% 2` and division `/ 2` to count bits, bypassing bitwise operators.
Student uses a signed integer `int` parameter, risking infinite loop with negative values if shifted arithmetically.
Student implements Brian Kernighan's algorithm (`n &= (n - 1)`) to clear the lowest set bit, reducing time complexity.
Student prints the bit count inside the function instead of returning it to the caller.
Student uses logical AND `&&` instead of bitwise AND `&` to mask bits, producing incorrect counts.
